title: The Octopus Mind
context:
For most of the twentieth century, invertebrates were regarded as simple creatures driven by reflex. The octopus has done much to overturn that view. Its nervous system contains roughly five hundred million neurons, a number comparable to that of a dog, yet only about a third of them are located in the brain. The remainder are spread through its eight arms, which can taste, touch and, to a surprising degree, make decisions without waiting for instructions from the centre.

Laboratory studies have documented the animal's capacity for learning. In a well-known series of experiments conducted in Naples in the 1950s, octopuses were trained to avoid a white square by receiving a mild shock when they attacked it, and they learned to ignore it within a few trials. Later researchers showed that captive octopuses could unscrew jar lids to reach food, a task that some mammals find difficult. Several aquarium keepers have also reported that individuals recognise particular staff members and squirt water at those they dislike.

Such abilities seem all the more remarkable given the animal's lifestyle. Most octopus species live only one to two years, and mothers typically die shortly after their eggs hatch, so young octopuses never meet their parents. They cannot, therefore, learn by imitation, as many birds and primates do. Whatever knowledge they gain must come from personal exploration. Some biologists suggest that this solitary upbringing explains why octopuses are so curious, although the hypothesis remains difficult to test.

Camouflage provides further evidence of sophistication. An octopus can change the colour and texture of its skin in under a second, matching a background of coral, sand or weed. Curiously, octopuses are thought to be colour-blind, as their eyes contain only a single type of light-sensitive pigment. How they match colours so accurately is therefore unexplained. One proposal is that the skin itself contains light-detecting proteins, allowing it to sense its surroundings directly, but this idea has not yet been confirmed in living animals. Divers who film octopuses on the seabed have also recorded them carrying coconut shells and later assembling them into portable shelters, behaviour that some scientists describe as a form of tool use. Others prefer a narrower definition of the term, so the label remains debated, and the same disagreement surrounds many other claims about invertebrate minds.

The practical implications are beginning to attract attention. Engineers designing soft robots have studied octopus arms because they can bend at any point, unlike jointed limbs. A prototype gripper modelled on the arm was able to pick up fragile objects such as eggs without breaking them. Meanwhile, ethicists argue that evidence of complex cognition should change the way octopuses are treated: in 2022 the United Kingdom extended legal recognition of sentience to octopuses, alongside crabs and lobsters. Critics of intensive octopus farming say that such legislation does not go far enough.

title: The Hanseatic League
context:
Between the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries, a network of north European trading towns known as the Hanseatic League dominated commerce across the Baltic and North Seas. It was never a state, and it had no capital, army or permanent officials. Instead, merchants from towns such as Lübeck, Hamburg and Danzig cooperated through shared rules, meeting occasionally at assemblies called diets to settle disputes and agree on common policy. At its height the League included well over a hundred towns.

The goods it carried were bulky and ordinary rather than luxurious. Timber, grain, furs and wax travelled west from the Baltic, while cloth and wine moved east. The most profitable single commodity was salted herring, which was essential for the many fast days of the medieval Christian calendar. Salt from Lüneburg was used to preserve the fish, and Lübeck's control of the salt route gave it a unique advantage over rival ports. Historians estimate that herring made up a large share of Lübeck's income, though precise figures are not available for most years.

Merchants abroad lived in fortified compounds called kontors, the most famous being the Steelyard in London and Bryggen in Bergen. Residents of these compounds were forbidden to marry local women and had to follow strict rules about trade, while young apprentices endured demanding initiation rituals. The compounds were privileged but resented by local traders, who complained that foreigners were taking profits out of the country. Occasionally this resentment turned violent. Life inside the compounds was also tightly regulated in everyday matters: the merchants ate together, locked the gates at night and kept their goods and records inside the walls. The arrangement protected them from theft and local disputes, but it also kept them apart from the towns in which they worked for decades, which did little to improve relations.

The League's power rested on collective action. When a ruler threatened its privileges, member towns could impose a trade embargo, refusing to supply goods until demands were met. In the 1360s the Danish king Valdemar attacked the island town of Visby; the towns responded by forming an alliance and, after a war, forced the king to sign the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370, which confirmed trading rights and gave the League a say in the Danish succession. Historians often regard this as the League's greatest triumph.

Decline came slowly. From the late fifteenth century, the Dutch developed larger, cheaper ships and offered competing services, while stronger national governments in England and Sweden wanted to keep trade profits for their own merchants. The discovery of Atlantic routes shifted the centre of European commerce westward. Although the last formal diet was held in 1669, only three towns attended. Today the heritage is still a matter of civic pride: Hamburg and Bremen continue to describe themselves officially as Hanseatic cities.

title: Forests in the Salt Water
context:
Mangrove forests grow along tropical and subtropical coasts, in places where salt water would kill most trees. Around eighty tree species have evolved to tolerate these conditions, and together they cover about 150,000 square kilometres worldwide, an area roughly equal to that of Bangladesh. Indonesia alone holds the largest single share of the total, although mangroves are found on every continent that has a warm coastline. The forests vary greatly in appearance. In sheltered river deltas the trees can grow to more than thirty metres, forming a closed canopy, while on exposed or very salty shores they may be little more than dense shrubs no taller than a person. Local conditions of salt, tide and sediment decide which of the two forms develops.

Mangroves have developed a range of strategies for coping with their environment. Some species excrete salt through their leaves, while others prevent most of it from entering at the roots. Because the mud in which they grow is waterlogged and contains almost no oxygen, many trees send up specialised roots that rise above the surface and take in air directly. Reproduction is equally unusual. In several species the seed begins to germinate while still attached to the parent tree; the young plant then drops into the water and floats until it lodges in mud, where it can root quickly.

The tangled roots create a sheltered nursery. Juvenile fish, crabs and prawns hide among them from larger predators, and many commercially important species spend only part of their lives in mangroves before moving to open water or reefs. Coastal communities have long gathered wood, honey and shellfish from these forests, and in some regions fishing families say that catches fall noticeably when nearby mangroves are cleared.

Mangroves also protect the land behind them. Their dense roots and trunks slow waves and reduce erosion. After the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, some studies suggested that villages sheltered by mangroves suffered fewer casualties, but other researchers have cautioned that the effect depends on the width of the forest belt and the size of the wave, and that no mangrove forest can stop a very large tsunami. A further benefit is climate related. Mangrove soils accumulate dead plant material that decays slowly in the absence of oxygen, so a hectare of mangrove locks away several times as much carbon as a hectare of most tropical forests, much of it below ground.

Despite these benefits, roughly one fifth of the world's mangroves have been lost since 1980. The main cause has been conversion to shrimp ponds, followed by agriculture and urban development. Efforts at restoration have had mixed results. Many planting schemes fail because seedlings are placed on mudflats where mangroves never grew naturally, or because the flow of tidal water that the trees need has been blocked. Projects that first restore the tides and then allow natural regrowth tend to do better. Some governments now pay coastal communities to guard remaining forests, although enforcement remains uneven.

title: The Promise of Small Loans
context:
Traditional banks have long avoided lending small sums to poor borrowers, arguing that the administrative cost of a tiny loan is the same as that of a large one while the risk of default seems higher. Microfinance emerged in the 1970s to challenge this assumption. Its best-known pioneer, the Bangladeshi economist Muhammad Yunus, began by lending a few dollars from his own pocket to a group of villagers who made bamboo stools, and found that they repaid on time. The amounts involved were tiny, hardly enough to buy bamboo for a week's work, yet they were large enough to free the villagers from dependence on local traders who bought their finished goods at very low prices. Yunus later argued that credit should be seen as a basic human right rather than a favour granted only to those who already own property. Banks, he said, had simply never tried to serve people without collateral.

The model that grew from this experiment relied on group lending. Borrowers formed small groups, and each member was responsible for encouraging the others to repay; if one person defaulted, the whole group could be refused further credit. Repayment rates reported by early programmes often exceeded 95 per cent. Most borrowers were women, partly because programme designers believed that women were more likely to spend their profits on food and schooling for their children.

Enthusiasm grew rapidly, and by the 2000s microfinance institutions served well over a hundred million clients. Yunus and the bank he founded shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006. Yet careful evaluation produced less dramatic results than the early stories had suggested. Randomised trials carried out in several countries found that access to small loans increased the number of tiny businesses but did not, on average, lift households out of poverty.

Critics identify other problems. Interest rates are often high, sometimes above thirty per cent a year, because the costs of serving small borrowers are real. In parts of India around 2010, competing lenders pushed loans on households that already had several, and a wave of over-indebtedness followed; the state of Andhra Pradesh passed emergency legislation restricting how lenders could collect repayments. Some officials blamed aggressive collectors for a number of suicides, although the link remains disputed.

Supporters respond that the loans were never meant as a cure for poverty on their own. They argue that credit helps families smooth their income, pay for emergencies and avoid moneylenders who charge far more. More recent programmes therefore combine loans with savings accounts, insurance and training. In East Africa, meanwhile, mobile phone payment services now allow tiny transactions at a fraction of the cost of a branch, and some analysts believe these will do more to widen access to finance than traditional microloans ever did.

title: What Happens While We Sleep
context:
Sleep occupies roughly a third of human life, yet for most of medical history it was regarded as a passive state. Since the 1950s, when researchers first recorded the electrical activity of sleeping brains, it has become clear that the brain remains highly active at night. Sleep proceeds in cycles lasting about ninety minutes, each containing lighter stages, deep slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. The amount of sleep that people need varies with age. Newborn babies sleep for most of the day, school-age children need around ten hours, and most adults function best on seven to nine, although a small minority seem to manage well on less. Doctors stress that the quality of sleep matters as much as its length.

Different stages seem to serve different purposes. Slow-wave sleep, which dominates the first half of the night, is associated with the consolidation of facts and events. In one widely cited experiment, students who learned lists of word pairs and then slept remembered more the next day than students who stayed awake for the same period. REM sleep, which becomes more frequent towards morning, appears important for emotional processing. Motor skills, such as finger-tapping sequences, tend to improve after a night of sleep even without further practice.

Sleep loss has measurable costs. Volunteers kept awake for twenty-four hours show reaction times comparable to those of people whose blood alcohol level is above the legal driving limit in many countries. Chronic short sleep has also been linked in large population studies to higher rates of obesity, heart disease and depression. However, such studies reveal only correlation, and it is hard to say whether poor sleep causes the illnesses or is a symptom of them.

Adolescents face a particular problem. The biological clock shifts later during the teenage years, so many teenagers naturally fall asleep after eleven at night and struggle to wake early. Several school districts in the United States that moved the start of the school day to after 8.30 a.m. reported improved attendance and fewer car accidents among students, although some schools found that pupils simply went to bed later and gained little extra sleep. A number of doctors have called for national guidelines on school start times.

For adults with chronic insomnia, sleeping pills offer short-term relief but are not recommended for long periods, because patients can become dependent on them and the drugs may reduce the proportion of deep sleep. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, delivered over several weeks, has been found in trials to be at least as effective as medication, and its benefits last longer. The main obstacle is a shortage of trained therapists, which has encouraged the development of online versions. Early results are encouraging, but information on long-term outcomes is limited.

title: Languages at Risk
context:
Linguists estimate that around seven thousand languages are spoken today, but the speakers are very unevenly distributed. Roughly forty per cent of languages have fewer than a thousand speakers, while a mere twenty-three languages account for more than half of the world's population. Some researchers predict that, without intervention, up to half of all languages could disappear by the end of this century. The most remarkable concentration of diversity is found on a single island in the Pacific, Papua New Guinea, where hundreds of languages are spoken by a population of only a few million people. In contrast, large countries with centralised education systems often have only a handful of widely used tongues.

Languages rarely die in a single dramatic moment. More often there is a gradual shift that unfolds over about three generations. Grandparents speak the heritage language fluently; their children understand it but reply in the majority language; and the grandchildren grow up knowing little of it. Economic pressure is usually the main driver, because parents come to believe that the majority language will offer their children better jobs. Policies have sometimes made matters worse. In parts of Wales and in boarding schools in North America, children were once punished for speaking their home languages, which sped up the decline.

Why does it matter? Some linguists point out that each language encodes local knowledge, such as the names of plants or the signs of coming weather, that may not translate easily into another tongue. Others argue that losing a language weakens a community's sense of identity. A third group replies that speakers themselves often choose to switch for practical reasons, and that outsiders should be cautious about imposing preservation on people who may not want it.

A few revivals have attracted wide attention. Hebrew became an everyday spoken language again during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, a remarkable achievement because for centuries it had been used mainly in religious texts. In New Zealand, Māori language nests, which were pre-schools where elders spoke only Māori with toddlers, began in 1982, and Māori became an official language of the country in 1987. Immersion schools have played a similar part in the recovery of Hawaiian.

Technology is now part of the discussion. Predictive keyboards, translation tools and speech recognition could make small languages more useful in daily life, but they depend on large quantities of written text, which most of the world's languages lack. As a result, major technology companies support only a few hundred languages in their products. Some communities also worry about outside firms recording their speakers and then owning the data. The United Nations has declared 2022 to 2032 an International Decade of Indigenous Languages, hoping to focus attention on the problem.

title: Printing in Three Dimensions
context:
Three-dimensional printing, also called additive manufacturing, builds objects layer by layer from a digital design. This contrasts with traditional machining, which cuts material away from a solid block. The first commercial machine, which used a technique called stereolithography, was patented in the mid-1980s by the American engineer Chuck Hull. For about two decades afterwards the technology was used almost exclusively to produce prototypes.

The expiry of several key patents around 2009 helped make cheap desktop printers possible, and a wave of publicity followed. Commentators in the 2010s predicted that most households would soon own a printer and make everyday objects at home. This did not happen. Printing even a simple item can take several hours, the quality of cheap plastic is limited, and for large quantities of identical goods conventional mass production remains far less expensive. Many early buyers also discovered that operating a printer demanded more patience and technical skill than the advertisements implied. Models had to be designed or downloaded, files repaired, and failed prints cleaned up, and a large share of the machines ended up unused in cupboards after the first few months. Even so, a small community of enthusiasts continued to share designs online, repairing and improving each other's machines and gradually raising the standard of what an inexpensive printer could produce.

The technology has instead found its place in specialised niches. In aerospace, an engine manufacturer redesigned a fuel nozzle that had been assembled from around twenty separate parts and now prints it as a single piece, which is lighter than the original. Printing is also well suited to products that are unique to each user. Hearing-aid shells and clear dental aligners, for example, are now almost always produced this way, because every ear and every set of teeth is different.

Medicine offers further possibilities. In bioprinting, machines deposit living cells in layers to build tissue, and researchers have succeeded in printing small pieces of cartilage in the laboratory. Complete organs with working blood vessels remain a distant goal, and none has been transplanted into a patient. More immediate progress has been made with prosthetics. Printed artificial hands for children can be made cheaply, which matters because children outgrow them quickly.

Construction firms in several countries have experimented with printing the walls of small houses from concrete. Critics point out that cement production has a high carbon footprint and that building regulations have not kept pace with the new methods. Metal printing, meanwhile, consumes large amounts of energy, and some of the fine powders used can be hazardous to breathe. Supporters argue that the process creates less waste, since material is added only where it is needed, and that spare parts can be printed on demand rather than stored in warehouses. Whether these savings outweigh the costs is still unproven.

title: The Secret of Roman Concrete
context:
Many Roman buildings are still standing after two thousand years. The Pantheon in Rome, completed in the second century AD, has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, spanning about forty-three metres. Modern concrete, by contrast, typically begins to deteriorate within decades, especially when its steel reinforcement rusts and expands. This contrast has made Roman concrete a subject of intense research. Engineers who maintain bridges and sea walls know that repairs to modern structures are costly and frequent, and some regard the question of how the ancient material endured as more than an academic puzzle. If its secrets could be understood, they argue, new buildings might be designed to last for centuries rather than for a single human lifetime.

The recipe used by Roman builders combined lime, volcanic ash and chunks of stone or brick. Vitruvius, an architect writing in the first century BC, recommended ash from the area around the Bay of Naples. When this ash is mixed with lime and water, it undergoes a chemical reaction that continues to strengthen the material long after it has set. The same mixture hardened even when placed in seawater, which allowed Roman engineers to build harbours and breakwaters directly into the sea.

Recent studies have focused on small white lumps of lime, known as clasts, that appear throughout the material. Earlier scholars considered them evidence of careless mixing. In 2023, however, a team of researchers at a university in the United States proposed that the clasts allow the concrete to repair itself. When a crack forms and water seeps in, the lime in the clasts dissolves and then recrystallises, filling the gap. To test the idea, the team made concrete using a hot mixing process with quicklime. Cracked samples healed within weeks, whereas control samples made without quicklime did not. Some archaeologists remain unconvinced that the Romans actually used hot mixing, because ancient texts seem to describe the use of slaked lime.

Design also contributed to the buildings' survival. Concrete resists compression well but is weak under tension, and the Romans, who did not use iron reinforcement in the way modern builders do, relied on arches, vaults and domes that keep the material squeezed together. In the Pantheon, the builders used heavier aggregate at the base of the dome and progressively lighter stone towards the top, and they carved recessed panels into the inner surface to reduce its weight.

Copying the Romans is not straightforward. Their concrete cured slowly, which does not suit modern construction schedules, and it cannot support the tall steel-framed structures that cities now demand. Yet the environmental argument is strong: cement production is responsible for around eight per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions. Several firms are therefore testing blends that replace part of the cement with volcanic ash. Whether such mixtures will last for centuries cannot yet be known, since modern versions have existed for only a few years.

title: Waiting for the Second Marshmallow
context:
In the late 1960s, the psychologist Walter Mischel and his colleagues at Stanford University offered preschool children a choice. They could eat one marshmallow immediately, or wait about fifteen minutes alone in a room and receive two. The experiment was designed to be simple. The child was left in a plain room with a table, a chair and the treat, and the researcher watched through a one-way window. Nothing else was provided, so that the only question was how long each child could hold out. Some children ate the sweet at once. Others waited, and many of these used strategies to cope, such as covering their eyes, singing quietly or turning their chairs away from the plate.

Years later, the researchers reported that the children who had waited longer had gone on to achieve higher scores in school entrance tests, and their parents rated them as better at coping with stress. The finding was widely publicised, and some parenting books suggested that self-control at the age of four predicts success in adult life. Yet the original sample was small, at around ninety children, and most of them came from families connected with the university. Many of the children also dropped out of the follow-up studies.

In 2018, a team of researchers repeated the experiment with a much larger group of about nine hundred children from more varied backgrounds. They found that the link between waiting time and later achievement was only about half as strong as in the original work. Moreover, it almost disappeared once the researchers took account of the families' income, the mother's education and the quality of the children's home environment. The authors concluded that a child's ability to wait reflects circumstances at least as much as any fixed personal quality.

Another experiment suggests how this might work. At the University of Rochester, children were first given a task in which an adult promised them better art supplies. For one group the adult returned with the supplies as promised; for the other group the adult returned empty-handed. In the marshmallow test that followed, children who had met a reliable adult waited an average of twelve minutes, while those who had met an unreliable adult waited an average of three. Waiting, in other words, can be a sensible decision when a child has reason to trust that the reward will arrive.

None of this means that self-control is unimportant. Classroom programmes that teach children strategies such as distraction have produced short-term improvements, but the gains often fade once the programme ends. Mischel himself later stressed strategies rather than willpower. Many researchers now argue that reducing temptation, for example by keeping sweets out of sight, is a more dependable approach than relying on resolve.

title: The Box That Changed Trade
context:
Until the middle of the twentieth century, cargo was loaded onto ships by hand. Sacks, barrels and crates were lifted aboard by teams of dockworkers, a process known as break-bulk shipping. Loading a single vessel could take a week, and a considerable share of the goods was damaged or stolen along the way. In April 1956 the American trucking entrepreneur Malcom McLean sent a converted tanker, the Ideal X, from Newark to Houston carrying fifty-eight metal containers. It was a modest beginning, but it opened a new era. McLean had no background in shipping, which may explain why he was willing to question habits that dockworkers and shipowners had accepted for generations. He had noticed while waiting at a port, so the story goes, that it would be simpler to lift the whole truck body than to unload its contents piece by piece.

McLean's key insight was that a box should be able to travel between truck, train and ship without ever being opened. His engineers designed strong corner fittings that allowed containers to be stacked high and locked together. At first, each shipping company used its own sizes, which limited the benefits, but international agreement on standard dimensions was reached in the 1960s, producing the familiar twenty-foot and forty-foot lengths. Once any container could fit any ship, truck or crane, the system became far more efficient.

The effect on costs was dramatic. Some estimates suggest that the cost of loading a tonne of cargo fell by more than ninety per cent. The war in Vietnam gave the new method a boost, since the American military needed vast quantities of supplies moved across the Pacific and found containers convenient. Ports that failed to adapt declined: the old docks close to the centre of London, which could not accommodate the new ships, gradually closed, and traffic shifted to deep-water terminals elsewhere. Dockworkers lost large numbers of jobs, and their unions resisted the change through strikes, though without lasting success.

Economists now argue that the container did more to expand international trade than many formal agreements. One well-known study concluded that the introduction of container shipping increased trade between countries by more than the reduction of tariffs achieved over the same period. By making transport cheap and predictable, it allowed manufacturers to divide production between several countries, with components crossing oceans before the final product was assembled.

The system has its own problems. The largest ships can now carry more than twenty thousand containers, but few ports have channels deep enough to receive them, and delays at crowded terminals can ripple through supply chains for months. Shipping accounts for around three per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, and regulators are pressing the industry to switch to cleaner fuels. Containers also fall overboard in storms; the industry reports that several hundred are lost at sea in an average year, although the figure varies widely from year to year.
